posted.why_it_matters: This PR adds a direct two-file cycle. ReactionsRow.tsx now imports the new ReactionsRowButtonViewModel (line 25), and ReactionsRowButtonViewModel.ts imports REACTION_SHORTCODE_KEY back from ReactionsRow (line 19). The new view model also imports ReactionsRowButtonTooltipViewModel, which already imported REACTION_SHORTCODE_KEY from ReactionsRow, so it forms a second loop. ReactionsRowButtonViewModel.ts is the file that joins the cycle. ReactionsRowButton.tsx leaves it because ReactionsRow no longer imports it. All of these imports are kept at runtime. That means the load order depends on which file is imported first. If a view model module loads first, ReactionsRow may still be only partly evaluated when the view model reads REACTION_SHORTCODE_KEY. The constant is only read inside functions, so this may not break right away. Still, the files are now tied together: none of them can load or be tested on its own, and a future top-level use of the constant could see it as undefined.

suggestions.text: Move REACTION_SHORTCODE_KEY (the UnstableValue constant) out of ReactionsRow.tsx into a small module that imports nothing from this group, for example src/components/views/messages/reactionShortcode.ts or a file under src/viewmodels/message-body/. Then have ReactionsRow.tsx, ReactionsRowButtonViewModel.ts and ReactionsRowButtonTooltipViewModel.ts all import it from there. Both loops go through a view model's import of ReactionsRow, so removing those imports should break both.
Another option: let ReactionsRow pass the shortcode lookup (or the resolved custom reaction name) into the view model as a prop. Then the view models never need to import ReactionsRow.

posted.why_it_matters: The PR adds a new file, src/viewmodels/timeline/DateSeparatorViewModel.tsx. That file has a runtime import of SdkContextClass from src/contexts/SDKContext.ts (line 30). MessageEditHistoryDialog.tsx now imports the view model (line 22) where it used to import DateSeparator. SDKContext.ts is already part of the large existing cycle: SDKContext → LegacyCallHandler → utils/notifications → Unread → EventTileFactory → MessageEvent → TextualBody → MessageEditHistoryDialog. So the new view model joins that cycle and makes it one file bigger. The cycle matters at load time. Depending on which file loads first, DateSeparatorViewModel.tsx can run before SDKContext.ts has finished, or the other way round. Then an imported binding is still undefined when it's read, or a module-level `class X extends Y` throws. Every file in the cycle now has to load in the right order, including this new one.

suggestions.text: Remove the runtime import of SdkContextClass from DateSeparatorViewModel.tsx. The view model only uses it inside pickDate, to call `SdkContextClass.instance.roomViewStore.getRoomId()`. You could pass that in through the props instead, for example a `getCurrentRoomId: () => string | undefined` callback or the RoomViewStore itself. The React component that creates the view model can get it from the SDKContext React context, so the view model file no longer needs to import contexts/SDKContext.

If you want to keep the current lookup, load SDKContext lazily inside pickDate with `const { SdkContextClass } = await import("../../contexts/SDKContext");`. That way the module isn't loaded when DateSeparatorViewModel.tsx loads. Then run rie check again to confirm the file has left the cycle.

Another option is to break the existing chain where it reaches the dialog: TextualBody.tsx imports MessageEditHistoryDialog statically just to open it. Loading the dialog lazily there, e.g. `Modal.createDialog(lazy(() => import("../dialogs/MessageEditHistoryDialog")))` or with a dynamic import in the click handler, would remove the TextualBody → MessageEditHistoryDialog edge. That fixes this loop, but other loops may still keep these files entangled.

posted.why_it_matters: This PR adds the new file src/controllers/comments.ts to an existing runtime import cycle of 79 files. That cycle already contains app.ts, server.ts, the services barrel and most controllers. Two new imports put it there. app.ts imports it (`import commentsRouter from './controllers/comments.js'`, line 19), and comments.ts imports `respond` from src/middleware/respond.ts (line 4). respond.ts already leads back to app.ts through this existing chain: services/import-export.ts → utils/get-service.ts → services/index.ts → services/server.ts → server.ts → app.ts. So comments.ts is both loaded by a cycle member and depends on one. Which module finishes loading first now depends on which file is loaded first. If comments.ts ran while respond.ts was still loading, `respond` would be undefined at the moment `router.post(..., respond)` and similar calls register the routes. This only grows the group by one file, and the other controllers already join it the same way through respond.ts. Even so, the check fails because the PR made the cycle bigger.

suggestions.text: Break the existing link instead of only the new one. respond.ts imports ExportService from services/import-export.ts, which reaches get-service.ts and the services barrel. If respond.ts loaded ExportService lazily (`await import('../services/import-export.js')` inside the export branch), comments.ts and every other controller would probably leave the cycle. This is a larger change than the PR itself and nobody has checked it.

Another option is to cut services/server.ts → server.ts (it imports only SERVER_ONLINE). Moving SERVER_ONLINE into a small standalone module that both server.ts and services/server.ts import would remove the path from the services barrel back to app.ts. That might break up much of the 79-file group.

If you want this PR to keep the cycle the same size and fix it later, a code-only change in comments.ts won't do it. It needs `respond`, and the only route to respond.ts goes into the cycle. The other way out is to register the comments router without a static import in app.ts, for example with a dynamic import inside createApp. That puts it out of step with how every other router is mounted.

posted.why_it_matters: Your PR adds `src/controllers/comments.ts`, and two new imports put it inside the existing runtime cycle. `src/app.ts` imports it (`import commentsRouter from './controllers/comments.js'`, line 19), and it imports `respond` from `src/middleware/respond.ts` (line 5). That makes the cycle one file bigger. At load time, ES modules in a cycle can run before the modules they depend on have finished running. A top-level value such as `respond` or a service class could still be uninitialized (a TDZ error, or undefined) when comments.ts runs `router.use(...)` and registers its routes, depending on which file in the loop loads first. The other controllers already import respond.ts the same way, so comments.ts follows an existing pattern. That pattern is the cycle the check measures.

suggestions.text: Break the shared loop at its weakest point, `src/services/server.ts` line 16 (`import { SERVER_ONLINE } from '../server.js'`). If SERVER_ONLINE lived in a small standalone module (or was read through a getter that server.ts calls) and services/server.ts imported it from there, services/server.ts would no longer import server.ts → app.ts. That should take comments.ts and the other controllers out of this cycle.

Another option is to remove the respond.ts → import-export.ts edge. respond.ts could load ExportService lazily (with `await import('../services/import-export.js')` inside the export branch) instead of importing it at the top level, so controllers that use `respond` no longer reach get-service.ts / services/index.ts when the module loads.

Delete the stray `import type * as rieTrap from "../app.js";` on line 1 of src/controllers/comments.ts. It is type-only and gets erased at compile time, so it is not part of this runtime loop, but nothing uses it and it adds a type-level edge back to app.ts.

posted.why_it_matters: Before this PR there was no import cycle here. The PR adds `import { getPermissionsForShare }` to fetch-permissions.ts at line 6. The new file get-permissions-for-share.ts imports `fetchPermissions` back from fetch-permissions.ts at line 8. It also imports `fetchAllowedFieldMap`, and fetch-allowed-field-map.ts already imported `fetchPermissions`. So three files now depend on each other at runtime: fetch-permissions.ts, get-permissions-for-share.ts and fetch-allowed-field-map.ts. Whichever of them loads first, it imports another file in the loop before it has finished evaluating. That other file can then see bindings from the first that haven't been initialized yet. Today every use is inside a function body, so this probably works. But the evaluation order now depends on which file the app happens to import first. Any top-level use added later, such as a `withCache(...)` wrapper or a re-export, could fail with a TDZ error or `undefined`. The loop also ties the core permission fetcher to share-specific logic.

suggestions.text: In fetch-permissions.ts, remove the static import at line 6 and load the module lazily where it's used: `const { getPermissionsForShare } = await import('../utils/get-permissions-for-share.js');`. fetch-share-info.ts in this same PR already does this for SharesService. The runtime edge then disappears from the static graph.

Take the share branch out of fetchPermissions so the core fetcher doesn't depend on share logic. Callers that have `accountability.share` (for example a wrapper function in a separate module) would call getPermissionsForShare themselves. get-permissions-for-share.ts can keep using fetchPermissions and fetchAllowedFieldMap without closing a loop.

Alternatively, pass the inner permission fetcher into getPermissionsForShare as a parameter instead of having it import fetchPermissions (dependency injection). Note that this only removes the direct two-file loop. The loop through fetch-allowed-field-map.ts would remain unless fetchAllowedFieldMap is injected or loaded lazily too.
